sections.h2: Where is Salisbury, Maryland, and why is it the hub of the Eastern Shore?
sections.html:
Salisbury is the county seat of Wicomico County and the largest city on Maryland's Eastern Shore, at the head of the Wicomico River on the Atlantic Coastal Plain. It is about 106 miles from Baltimore, 119 miles from Washington and 128 miles from Philadelphia.

The river is what built the town. Salisbury also has a working port: the Port of Salisbury is the second largest and second busiest commercial port in Maryland.

sections.h2: What is the history behind Salisbury's older neighborhoods?
sections.html:
Salisbury began in 1732 as a small colonial outpost set up by Lord Baltimore, and it was incorporated as a city in 1854. Wicomico County was formed in 1867, with Salisbury as its seat.

Fire shaped the old downtown. Blazes in 1860 and 1886 burned about two-thirds of the town. In 1909 the Humphreys Dam burst and flooded parts of the city.

Three historic areas are protected by the city: Camden, Newtown and Downtown. Houses there are covered by a separate review step for exterior changes, described below. Neighborhoods such as Rose and Lake Street have also been the focus of revitalization work.

Salisbury's economy is built on poultry, health care, education and distribution. Perdue Farms is headquartered in the city and is the largest employer based there, with nearly 22,000 employees overall.

  • Peninsula Regional Medical Center employs more city residents than any other company.
  • Salisbury University is another large employer.
  • Verizon, The Knowland Group, Handy Seafood and Pepsi Bottling of Delmarva also have a presence.
  • Other industries include foodservice, electronics, pharmaceuticals, shipbuilding and agriculture.

The Salisbury area had the seventh fastest job growth in the nation in 2016, at 4.2%.

sections.h2: How do roads, air and transit connect Salisbury?
sections.html:
U.S. 13 runs north and south toward Dover and Norfolk, and U.S. 50 runs east and west toward Ocean City and the Baltimore and Washington region. The Salisbury Bypass routes both around the city, and Maryland Routes 12 and 349 also serve it.

Wicomico Regional Airport has daily American Eagle service to Philadelphia and Charlotte. Shore Transit runs local buses, Greyhound offers intercity service, and the Delmarva Central Railroad carries freight.

sections.h2: What is the climate in Salisbury, and what should a house owner watch for?
sections.html:
Salisbury has a humid subtropical climate. Normals for 1991 to 2020 at the Wicomico Regional Airport show about 47.49 inches of precipitation and about 8.0 inches of snow a year, with a July average of 77.9 degrees and a January average of 36.8 degrees.

The city sits at 17 to 45 feet above sea level on the head of a river, so water is the main concern, and the 1909 dam failure is the local reminder. A tornado rated EF1 struck the city on August 7, 2017, with peak intensity over Dogwood Park. If your house has roof or tree damage from a past storm, say so when you describe it.

The city has several green spaces, including City Park, Riverwalk Park, Waterside Park and the Naylor Mill Forest Trail, which covers more than 92 acres and is the largest conservation easement inside a Maryland municipality.

sections.h2: What must a Salisbury owner file when a property changes hands?
sections.html:
Salisbury asks the owner to sign a Property Affidavit, sworn before a notary, and file it with the city's Internal Services Office before the deed is stamped.

  • The owner acknowledges city codes, including the property maintenance, plumbing and building codes.
  • The owner states the proposed use: owner-occupied, rental, commercial, a care or recovery-type residence, or other.
  • If the property will be rented, the owner must register the unit and get a rental license within 60 days of ownership or of it becoming a rental. The affidavit lists a $500 fine for failing to comply.
  • For homes in the Camden, Newtown or Downtown historic districts, exterior changes need a certificate of approval from the Salisbury Historic District Commission.

This is a form the buyer's side usually handles, but the seller should know it exists so the closing does not stall.

sections.h2: How do Salisbury's rental and vacant building rules work?
sections.html:
Salisbury requires a Rental Owner's License before any unit is registered. The first-year license costs $120 and renews for $75, and each unit costs $120 to register and $75 to renew. Renewals are due March 1 each year through the city's OpenGov portal.

  • New units must pass inspection before a license is issued, and failed units get a Corrective Action Letter.
  • A reinspection costs $100 if required.
  • Each business entity, such as an LLC, needs its own license and registrations.
  • Pre-1978 properties need a lead certificate uploaded at renewal and for new tenants.
  • Vacant residential buildings must be registered for $200 a year, with a $100 inspection after year one.

Code citations range from $25 to $500 per day depending on the violation, and unpaid fines or abatement costs can become a lien on the property. A vacant, unregistered or unlicensed house can carry these costs without the owner realizing it, so check the city record before you price a sale.

sections.h2: How does property tax work for a house inside Salisbury?
sections.html:
A Salisbury homeowner receives two bills, one from Wicomico County and one from the City of Salisbury. The city began billing its own taxes with fiscal year 2019 to 2020, after the county ended its contract to process the city's bills.

The state's fiscal 2026 table lists a county rate of 0.8099 and a city rate of 1.0332, for a combined 1.8431. Property just outside the city but in the county carries only the county rate.

  • Wicomico County taxes are collected by the Wicomico Department of Finance at 125 N. Division Street, Salisbury.
  • City taxes are handled by the City Finance Department, which gave 410-548-3110 as its number in a 2020 notice. Confirm it is still current.
  • Wicomico County does not currently impose a county transfer tax, though state law allows up to 1%, according to the state's 2026 guide.

Maryland reassesses each property every three years and phases the increase in equally over three years. An appeal of a new assessment must be filed within 45 days of the notice date with the local assessment office.

sections.h2: What do Salisbury sellers usually deal with, and where does a cash sale fit?
sections.html:
Sellers who own rental houses, inherited houses or houses with deferred repairs face the licensing and code steps above. A listing can stall while the owner sorts those items out.

A cash buyer can purchase the property as it is, but the legal steps remain: the affidavit, a clean title and any rental registration the city requires. Ask for a written offer, read the closing terms, and have your own settlement company confirm each item before you sign.

faqs.q: Is Salisbury, MD the county seat of Wicomico County?
faqs.a: Yes. Salisbury became the seat when Wicomico County was formed in 1867. It is the largest city on Maryland's Eastern Shore.

faqs.q: Does Salisbury bill its own property tax?
faqs.a: Yes. Starting with fiscal year 2019 to 2020, owners get one bill from the City of Salisbury and a separate one from Wicomico County. The 2026 state table lists city and county real property rates of 1.0332 and 0.8099.

faqs.q: Do I need a rental license to sell a rented house in Salisbury?
faqs.a: A rental owner must hold a license and register each unit, and a buyer who keeps the house as a rental must do the same within 60 days of ownership. Ask the city whether your current registration is in good standing before you sell.

faqs.q: What is the Salisbury Property Affidavit?
faqs.a: It is a sworn form the owner files with the city's Internal Services Office before the deed is stamped. It confirms the proposed use of the property and acknowledges city codes, rental registration and historic district rules.

faqs.q: What can Salisbury fine for code violations?
faqs.a: City code citations range from $25 to $500 per day depending on the violation and offense. Unpaid fines or abatement costs can become a lien on the property.
